clue.text: Blunder made by No.10, maybe, in the air

parts.note: screws are sold by gauge number, so a No.10 is one size of screw; the surface wants it to be Downing Street
something held in the air is up, raised aloft

explanation.surface: A political gaffe dreamed up at Downing Street that is now hanging over the government.
explanation.walkthrough: No.10 reads as the Prime Minister's address, but here it is a screw size.
explanation.definitionFit: A screw-up is informal slang for a bungled job or serious mistake.

clue.text: Frank scoffed — but he didn't fare too well as one

definitions.note: stands for the answer itself, the thing Frank stood as

parts.note: candid means frank, outspoken
to scoff food is to eat it greedily

explanation.surface: Frank Dobson, mocked for his lacklustre run as Labour's London mayoral nominee.
explanation.walkthrough: Frank is Frank Dobson, Labour's candidate who came third in the 2000 London mayoral election; here frank is an adjective.
explanation.definitionFit: A candidate is a person standing for election, which is what one refers back to.

clue.text: 'Listener' insert with Brenda grabbing a bit of publicity

indicators.note: the outer letters grab hold of the other, holding it inside

parts.note: Private Eye's nickname for the Queen, so ER, Elizabeth Regina
a plug is a brief promotional mention

explanation.surface: An insert in The Listener magazine, with the Queen featuring in a promotional piece.
explanation.walkthrough: Brenda is Private Eye's long-running nickname for Queen Elizabeth II. The Listener was a BBC magazine; here a listener is an ear.
explanation.definitionFit: An earplug is something inserted into the ear, the organ of a listener.

clue.text: Relax — university gets Brown finally on news

indicators.note: only the end of the word is used, its last letter

parts.note: the last letter of the word Brown
to get wind of something is to hear news of it

explanation.surface: A university is told to calm down once Gordon Brown makes an announcement.
explanation.walkthrough: Brown is Gordon Brown, then Chancellor; only its last letter counts.
explanation.definitionFit: To unwind is to loosen up and stop being tense.

clue.text: It's not pussy Pat's treated with ice

indicators.note: letters that are treated are processed and changed, so these are reordered

explanation.surface: Pat's wound is being cleaned up with ice so it does not fester.
explanation.walkthrough: Pussy here is pus-sy, full of pus, not the cat or anything ruder.
explanation.definitionFit: An aseptic wound is sterile, free from the infection that produces pus.

clue.text: Rumpus not unfamiliar in this parliament?

parts.note: a storm is an uproar or outcry

indicators.note: a familiar word made strange, so its letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: Uproar is a regular feature of this assembly's sittings.
explanation.walkthrough: Stormont is the seat of the Northern Ireland Assembly, newly restored at the time.
explanation.definitionFit: Stormont is the building in Belfast that houses the Northern Ireland Assembly, so it stands for that legislature.

clue.text: It's academic: classy Mowlam's a scandalous politician!

parts.note: prof is short for professor
U means upper-class, from the U and non-U usage debate
Mo Mowlam, the Labour cabinet minister, was always known as Mo

explanation.surface: A claim that Mo Mowlam's scandal is purely theoretical.
explanation.walkthrough: U for upper-class comes from 1950s talk of U and non-U speech.
explanation.definitionFit: John Profumo was the minister whose 1963 affair with Christine Keeler became a famous British political scandal.

clue.text: As one might say on entering old architect familiarly

definitions.text: As one might say on entering
definitions.meaning: first meaning: split into three words, it is the jaunty phrase a person calls out while stepping through a doorway
second meaning: the first name of a 17th-century English architect

explanation.surface: A greeting someone might use on walking in to meet a historic architect.
explanation.walkthrough: Split as in I go, it is what someone says on walking in; run together it is Inigo Jones's first name, hence familiarly.
explanation.definitionFit: Inigo Jones designed the Banqueting House in Whitehall, and friends would call him by his first name.

clue.text: Making a mockery of transporting your urine sample?

definitions.meaning: first meaning: British slang for mocking or making fun
second meaning, taken literally: carrying the stuff to the clinic

explanation.walkthrough: The British idiom for ridiculing someone, read literally as carrying urine to the doctor.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom means ridiculing someone; literally it describes conveying a specimen to be tested.

clue.text: As a royal, "one pulled"

parts.note: an is the indefinite article, meaning one
drew as in drew a cart or drew a curtain, the past tense of draw

explanation.surface: A royal described as someone who has pulled, a jibe at a prince's reputation with women.
explanation.walkthrough: Pulled also has the British slang sense of picking someone up romantically, which fits Prince Andrew's tabloid image.
explanation.definitionFit: Prince Andrew is a member of the British royal family, the Queen's second son.

clue.text: Charlie's game to penetrate an Italian girl as a form of defence of one's conduct

definitions.text: a form of defence of one's conduct

indicators.note: one piece goes into another, so the sport is placed inside the girl's letters

parts.note: the article an gives the letter A, its one-letter form
Gia is an Italian girl's name, a short form of Gianna
Prince Charles was a keen polo player

explanation.surface: Prince Charles's love life is explained away as a justification of his behaviour.
explanation.walkthrough: Charlie is Prince Charles, famous for playing polo.
explanation.definitionFit: An apologia is a formal written justification of one's opinions or behaviour.

clue.text: Time to take spanner to this moving example of modern engineering!

definitions.text: this moving example of modern engineering

indicators.note: one piece takes the next alongside it, so the two are joined in order

parts.note: a millennium is a period of a thousand years
a bridge spans a river, so it is a spanner

explanation.surface: A wobbly new structure so poorly built that a mechanic with a spanner is needed to fix it.
explanation.walkthrough: London's Millennium Bridge opened in June 2000 and closed within days because it swayed alarmingly underfoot. Spanner looks like the tool; it is something that spans.
explanation.definitionFit: The London footbridge became notorious for swaying, so moving describes its wobble as well as its novelty.

clue.text: Crafty observation of a crank?

parts.note: read crafty as to do with a flying craft: the kind of sighting an eccentric reports

explanation.surface: A sly remark made about some eccentric person.
explanation.walkthrough: Crafty means sly on the surface; here it means to do with a spacecraft.
explanation.definitionFit: A UFO is an unidentified flying object, the alien spacecraft that cranks claim to have spotted.

clue.text: Grotty bloke next to gutless bloke

indicators.note: one piece is set right beside the other, a plain joining

parts.note: bloke is British slang for a man

indicators.note: the guts are the inside, so the middle letter of the word is removed

parts.note: guy is another informal word for a man

explanation.surface: One scruffy man standing beside another man with no courage.
explanation.walkthrough: Grotty is British slang for shabby or unpleasant.
explanation.definitionFit: Mangy literally means scabby with mange, and figuratively shabby and squalid.

clue.text: One drink with date results in celebrated engagement

parts.note: gin is a spirit
to court someone is to go out with them romantically

explanation.surface: A single drink on a date that ends in a much-celebrated betrothal.
explanation.walkthrough: Engagement suggests marriage after the date; it means a battle.
explanation.definitionFit: Agincourt, Henry V's 1415 victory over the French, is a famous battle, and an engagement is a military clash.

clue.text: When MPs break Tony's heart, one enters a state of depression

indicators.note: the single letter goes into the gap within the other pieces

parts.note: Parliament's holidays are called recesses

indicators.note: the heart of a word is its middle letters

explanation.surface: MPs go on holiday and Tony Blair's spirits sink into gloom.
explanation.definitionFit: A recession is an economic downturn, and a depression is a severe slump.

clue.text: Hostile and vile turn-off

indicators.note: something gone off has spoiled and changed, so the letters are reworked

explanation.surface: Something nasty and aggressive that puts you right off.
explanation.walkthrough: Turn-off looks like one noun; it splits into fodder and signal.
explanation.definitionFit: Virulent means bitterly hostile or venomous, as in virulent criticism.

clue.text: Perhaps Sir Trevor McDonald's heard rival late TV spot

indicators.note: what is heard is spoken, so the phrase is replaced by one with the same sound

parts.note: the ITN newsreader was knighted, so he is an example of a news knight

explanation.surface: Sir Trevor McDonald's late-night news slot faces a rival programme on another channel.
explanation.walkthrough: Sir Trevor McDonald read ITV's News at Ten; Newsnight is the BBC's late-evening current affairs programme.
explanation.definitionFit: Newsnight is a BBC Two current affairs show broadcast late in the evening, competing with ITV's news.

clue.text: Speaker might stand on this TV series package

parts.note: a soap opera is a long-running television drama
a box is a container for posting

explanation.surface: A TV series sold as a set for viewers to stand on.
explanation.walkthrough: Speaker suggests the Commons Speaker or a loudspeaker; it is a street orator.
explanation.definitionFit: Street orators traditionally stood on an upturned crate to address crowds.

clue.text: Punch's pointless, piss-poor pieces

indicators.note: something done badly is botched, so the remaining letters are jumbled
E for east is a compass point, and one of them is dropped from the word

explanation.surface: A jibe at Punch magazine for printing worthless articles.
explanation.walkthrough: Punch was the British humour magazine Private Eye loved to mock; here it is the noun meaning zest.
explanation.definitionFit: Punch in the sense of vigour or zest is a synonym of spice, the thing that adds interest.

clue.text: Devoted traveller left off contraceptive — ghastly

indicators.note: left gives L, and off means it is removed

parts.note: the pill is the oral contraceptive
grim means dreadful

explanation.surface: A traveller came off the pill with awful consequences.
explanation.walkthrough: Left looks like a verb in the surface; it is L for left.
explanation.definitionFit: A pilgrim is a religious traveller journeying to a shrine out of devotion.

clue.text: See 12
Seedy thing reportedly taken by a peer

indicators.note: a report is spoken, so a word sounding the same is taken

parts.note: a pee is what someone who pees takes; peer is read as one who pees, not a lord

explanation.surface: Something dodgy accepted by a member of the House of Lords.
explanation.walkthrough: Seedy means disreputable on the surface but literally a seed here; peer is a lord on the surface.
explanation.definitionFit: A pea is the round seed of the pea plant, eaten as a vegetable.

clue.text: Rubbished Europe endlessly like Hague? Well, no, actually

indicators.note: something rubbished is trashed and broken up, so its letters are rearranged
the word loses its end, its last letter

explanation.surface: William Hague trashing Europe, a reminder he is hardly a fan.
explanation.walkthrough: William Hague, Tory leader in 2000, was a Eurosceptic, so the definition's well, no, actually says he is the opposite.
explanation.definitionFit: Pro-EU means in favour of the European Union, the stance Hague famously did not hold.

clue.text: Having an erection for every set from 'Posh'

parts.note: something erect is up
per as in per person
a class is a set or group of people

explanation.surface: A ribald line about Posh Spice and the effect she has on men in her circle.
explanation.walkthrough: Posh suggests Victoria Beckham, Posh Spice, but it is the adjective.
explanation.definitionFit: Posh means smart and associated with the highest social stratum.

clue.text: The last men's bollocks

definitions.meaning: first meaning: shoemakers, who shape shoes on a last
second meaning: nonsense, from rhyming slang ...' awls for balls

explanation.walkthrough: A last is a shoemaker's foot-shaped mould, not the final ones; British slang uses the answer for both testicles and rubbish.
explanation.definitionFit: Shoemakers who mend footwear on a last, and British slang for nonsense through rhyming slang cobblers' awls.

clue.text: Blair's barrackers embraced by cussed naturalist

indicators.note: one piece is held inside the other, so the barrackers go within the oath

parts.note: darn is a mild curse, so darn means cussed
the Women's Institute slow-handclapped Tony Blair at its conference in June 2000

explanation.surface: A grumpy nature lover hugging the women who heckled the Prime Minister.
explanation.walkthrough: The WI is the Women's Institute, a British countrywomen's organisation that famously heckled Blair.
explanation.definitionFit: Charles Darwin was the Victorian naturalist who proposed evolution by natural selection.

clue.text: Don rather goes without kiss, love

indicators.note: the outer word goes on the outside of the others, wrapping them

parts.note: quite as in quite good, meaning somewhat
a cross is the written symbol for a kiss
love is zero in tennis, which looks like the letter

explanation.surface: A university fellow who would rather do without affection.
explanation.walkthrough: Don suggests an Oxbridge tutor or a verb for putting on clothes; it is the Spanish title.
explanation.definitionFit: Don Quixote is Cervantes' knight, so the title Don goes with this name.

clue.text: The country, full of bacteria, entraps one

indicators.note: the outer word traps the other inside it

parts.note: germy means teeming with germs
an is the indefinite article, meaning one

explanation.surface: A grim picture of rural Britain, full of infection and catching someone in it.
explanation.walkthrough: The country suggests the countryside; it means a particular nation.
explanation.definitionFit: Germany is a nation in central Europe.
